name: xplanet
desc: Create HQ wallpapers of planet Earth
why: Renders planets as wallpapers from real astronomical data, a pleasant old-school trick, though the output is mostly pretty.

brief.what_it_is: Xplanet is a free, GPL-licensed program that renders an image of a planet, moon, or the Sun and either draws it to an X window, saves it to a file (gif, jpg, png, ppm, tiff), or sets it as the desktop wallpaper. Its inputs are command-line options and an optional configuration file, along with map and star images and, for precise positions, JPL ephemeris or SPICE kernel files. The output is a rendered picture of the chosen body as seen from a chosen observer position, date, and projection. Earth is the default body.
brief.why_it_exists: Xplanet was inspired by Xearth, which renders an image of the earth into the X root window. The author's homepage says all of the major planets and most satellites can be drawn, similar to the Solar System Simulator.
brief.how_it_works: The program places an observer at a chosen location and time relative to a target body, then computes the view and shading. Position data comes from a built-in model or from JPL ephemeris or SPICE files, and the view can be a globe or one of many map projections (azimuthal, Lambert, Mercator, Mollweide, orthographic, rectangular and others). Background stars come from a star map file, and output can be rerun on a timer with -wait or -num_times.

commands_seen.context: Centers the field of view on NAIF ID -82, which the README says is the Cassini orbiter. Requires SPICE support compiled in and the kernels present.
Centers the field of view on NORAD ID 20580, which the README says is the Hubble Space Telescope. Requires the appropriate TLE files.
Places the observer at the center of the Sun while targeting Earth. The README notes that -origin -sun instead places the observer on the far side of Earth from the Sun.
Places the observer where the Moon appears 3 degrees to the left of Earth.
Uses the given date (assumed GMT) instead of the current time.
Writes to a file instead of a window. The format comes from the extension and the default size is 512 by 512 pixels.
Sets the image geometry in X syntax, for example 256x256-10+10. The README uses this with -window or -output.
Runs a command before each render. The README example is xplanet.exe -prev_command ./prev.bat on Windows.
Selects a map projection such as mollweide or mercator. The README says multiple bodies are not shown when this option is used.
Rotates the globe counterclockwise. The README says -rotate 180 suits Southern Hemisphere viewers.

brief.install_notes: The homepage's own description implies a compile step: it lists several optional features that depend on build-time libraries or kernels, including the X Screensaver extension (for -idlewait and -hibernate), Pango (for -pango), SPICE (for -body naif-N), and image format libraries. Satellite and SPICE use needs extra data files: JPL ephemeris files (DE200, DE405 or DE406) for -ephemeris_file, SPICE kernels with a README in the spice subdirectory, and TLE files for norad IDs. Input files are found by searching the current directory, then -searchdir, then ~/.xplanet on X11, ~/Library/Xplanet on macOS, and DATADIR/xplanet, where DATADIR defaults to /usr/local/share. The homepage links to Maps & Scripts and Cloud Maps pages, which I did not fetch, so I can't say what map images are needed. I did not check the Homebrew formula.
brief.standout: It descends from Xearth but reaches further: many bodies, a wide range of projections, real ephemeris and spacecraft-tracking input, and cloud-overlay map generation. Its option set is large enough to work as a small astronomy visualizer rather than only a desktop picture.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage and option reference describe old platforms (FreeBSD 5.1, Sparc Solaris, Cygwin, Mac OS X Aqua) and have no release date or changelog visible in what I fetched. The sourceforge hosting and the Homebrew formula suggest it still packages, but I found no last-release or last-commit date.
brief.caveats: The homepage's tested platforms are old (i386 GNU/Linux, Sparc Solaris, FreeBSD 5.1, Cygwin, Darwin, Mac OS X Aqua). The README warns that -pango appears to leak memory, so it should not run indefinitely. -fork on Windows can leave multiple processes running unnoticed. Only TrueType fonts are supported. Satellite and SPICE features need extra data files and a build with those options. License is GPL, per the homepage.
quotes: Xplanet was inspired by Xearth, which renders an image of the earth into the X root window.
My friends in the Southern Hemisphere can use -rotate 180 to make the earth look like it should!
Be careful when using this option; it's easy to have multiple processes running at the same time without knowing it - check the Task Manager.

entry.title: xplanet
entry.tldr: Renders a shaded image of Earth, another planet, or the Moon as seen from any chosen place and date, then saves it or sets it as your wallpaper.
entry.deeper_look:
Xplanet draws a planet, moon, or the Sun from a chosen observer position and time. It can paint into an X window, write an image file (gif, jpg, png, ppm, tiff), or set the desktop background. Earth is the default target. You choose the date, the viewpoint, and whether you see a globe or a flat map in one of many projections: Mercator, Mollweide, Lambert, orthographic, azimuthal and others.

It was inspired by Xearth, which put an image of the Earth in the X root window. Xplanet goes further. The homepage says all the major planets and most satellites can be drawn. Positions come from a built-in model, or from JPL ephemeris and SPICE kernel files if you want precise ones. With the right data files you can center the view on a spacecraft such as Cassini or on Hubble, using NORAD IDs and TLE files.

The idea underneath is that a picture of the sky is a computation: put an observer somewhere, pick a time, and work out what is lit and what is in shadow. Changing the observer lets you see Earth from the Sun, or with the Moon 3 degrees to one side. With -wait or -num_times it re-renders on a timer, so the wallpaper follows real time.
entry.install:
brew install xplanet
Spacecraft and SPICE features need extra data files (JPL ephemeris, SPICE kernels, TLE files) and a build with those options. Map images are searched for in the current directory, then -searchdir, then ~/.xplanet on X11 or ~/Library/Xplanet on macOS.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the large set of command-line options.
Renders the Earth as it looks right now and saves it to a PNG instead of opening a window.
Renders Earth from a point where the Moon appears 3 degrees to its left.

entry.whats_unique: It descends from Xearth but covers many bodies, many map projections, and real ephemeris and spacecraft-tracking input. The option set is big enough to make it a small astronomy visualizer, not just a wallpaper tool.
entry.caveats: The documentation describes old platforms such as FreeBSD 5.1 and Sparc Solaris, no recent release date is visible, and the README warns that -pango appears to leak memory.
